1. Executive Summary

APT35, also known as Magic Hound, is a highly sophisticated, Iran-backed advanced persistent threat (APT) group active since at least 2014. Renowned for its targeted cyberattacks, APT35 focuses on strategic espionage, data exfiltration, and disruption operations primarily against organizations in the energy, government, and technology sectors. The group exhibits a particular emphasis on entities based in or connected to Saudi Arabia, leveraging advanced tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to achieve its objectives. APT35’s persistent and evolving threat profile underscores its status as a critical cyber adversary with global reach.

3. Geopolitical Targeting

APT35’s operations demonstrate a broad geopolitical footprint, with a primary focus on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, complemented by selective targeting across Europe, the Americas, and the Asia-Pacific. Affected countries include:

4. Targeted Sectors

APT35 demonstrates a strategic focus on critical industries and institutions, employing tailored cyberattacks to achieve espionage and disruption objectives. Key targeted sectors include:

  • Government Agencies: Foreign ministries, interior ministries, and other high- value government entities, particularly in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Western Europe.
  • Energy Sector: Major energy companies, with a pronounced emphasis on firms in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
  • Telecommunications: Providers in the Gulf region and Western Europe, often targeted for network access and data interception.
  • Defense Contractors: Organizations in the United States, United Kingdom, and Gulf nations, focusing on sensitive military and technological intelligence.
  • Media and Journalism: Outlets and individuals, frequently compromised through impersonation and phishing campaigns.
  • Academic Institutions: Think tanks and research bodies, especially those specializing in Middle Eastern studies, geopolitics, or nuclear security.
  • Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs): Human rights groups and civil society organizations, often aligned with Iran’s strategic interests.
  • Information Technology and Cybersecurity: Vendors targeted for credential harvesting and as staging points for broader network attacks.
  • Financial Services: Firms exploited for infrastructure targeting or to circumvent international sanctions.
  • Legal Sector: Law firms and consultancies involved in sanctions-related litigation or international legal matters.

Multi-Stage Attacks and Cross-Platform Espionage

Recent Activity and Escalation (2023–2024)

APT35 has significantly escalated its operations in 2023 and 2024, deploying increasingly sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to infiltrate high-value targets. The

group has refined its attack methodologies, leveraging advanced tools and multi-stage infection chains to enhance stealth and efficacy.

  • Notable Malware and Tools: APT35 has introduced new malware variants, including BellaCiao and its C++-based successor, BellaCPP, alongside enhancements to its Powerstar (CharmPower) backdoor. These tools enable persistent access and data exfiltration.
  • Attack Techniques: In 2024, the group exploited cloud hosting providers, malicious LNK files, and password-protected archives to bypass detection and deliver payloads. These multi-stage infection chains reflect APT35’s adaptability and focus on evading modern security defenses.
  • Victim Profile: Targets include foreign affairs ministries, think tanks, nuclear security experts, journalists, academics, and civil society organizations. APT35 prioritizes individuals and entities with strategic relevance to Iran’s geopolitical objectives, underscoring its role in state-sponsored espionage. [1][2][6]

6. Key Actors and Infrastructure

APT35, also known as Charming Kitten, relies on a network of skilled individuals and supporting infrastructure to execute its sophisticated cyber operations. The group’s key actors, notably Behzad Mesri, Mohammadamin Keshvari (alias ArYaIeIrAn), and Mohammad Rasoul Akbari, leverage their expertise and connections to Iranian web hosting services, such as Mahanserver, to facilitate state-sponsored cyberattacks. These actors are linked through social media interactions and operational roles, forming a coordinated network integral to APT35’s campaigns.

Behzad Mesri (Alias: Skote Vahshat)

  • Profile: Behzad Mesri, operating under the alias Skote Vahshat, is a prominent cybercriminal charged by the FBI and U.S. Department of Justice for orchestrating the 2017 HBO cyberattack. A former member of the Turk Black Hat Security group, Mesri has a history of defacing hundreds of websites globally, showcasing his technical proficiency.
  • HBO Attack (2017): Beginning in May 2017, Mesri infiltrated HBO’s internal network, exfiltrating over 1.5 terabytes of sensitive data, including unreleased Game of Thrones episodes, scripts, and other proprietary content. He demanded a $6 million Bitcoin ransom, launching a public campaign dubbed “HBO is Falling”

when HBO refused. Mesri created a dedicated leak site and contacted journalists to amplify the breach’s impact. HBO offered a $250,000 bug bounty, which he rejected.

  • Ties to Iran: U.S. authorities have linked Mesri to Iranian military cyber operations, indicating his role in state-sponsored activities. He remains at large in Iran, evading extradition.

Mohammadamin Keshvari (Alias: ArYaIeIrAn)

  • Profile: Operating under aliases such as aryaieiran@gmail.com, aryaieiran@hotmail.com, and mno_1988_fgh@yahoo.com (mailto:_1988_fgh@yahoo.com), ArYaIeIrAn is a 29-year-old Iranian hacker and Turk Black Hat member. His profile on the “Iranian Engineers Club” and documented website defacements on Zone-H confirm his malicious activities.

7. Campaign History

Charming Kitten group unleashes its new NokNok malware

Charming Kitten has evolved its attack strategy, now targeting macOS systems with new "NokNok" malware delivered via LNK files instead of its traditional malicious Word documents. This technical pivot is supported by a sophisticated social engineering scheme where attackers impersonate U.S. nuclear experts to build trust with their targets. The campaign demonstrates the adaptability of this cyber-espionage group, which has been linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Charming Kitten sends a malicious link containing a Google Script macro that redirects the victim to a Dropbox URL. The Dropbox source hosts a password-protected RAR archive containing a malware dropper that utilizes PowerShell code and an LNK file to stage the malware from a cloud hosting provider.

The final payload, known as GorjolEcho, is a backdoor that executes commands received from remote operators. To avoid suspicion, GorjolEcho opens a relevant PDF document related to previous discussions with the target.

Charming Kitten employs a different approach. After realizing the target is using macOS, they send a link to a site hosting a ZIP file disguised as a RUSI (Royal United Services Institute) VPN app

Fake RUSI VPN site dropping the NokNok malware : Upon executing the Apple script file within the archive, a curl command retrieves the NokNok payload, establishing a backdoor on the victim’s system.

NokNok collects system information, encrypts it, encodes it in base64 format, and exfiltrates it. It is suspected that NokNok may possess additional espionage-related functionality based on similarities to previously analyzed GhostEcho malware.

https://otx.alienvault.com/pulse/64c7996c41a419dcc173d2bb/ APT35 Targets Israel with Fake Meetings and Advanced Phishing

In mid-2025, during rising tensions between Iran and Israel, Iranian state-sponsored hackers linked to APT35 (Educated Manticore/Charming Kitten) launched a new spear-phishing campaign. The targets were Israeli journalists, cybersecurity experts, and professors.

Attackers pretended to be assistants or researchers and reached out via email and WhatsApp, using fake meeting invites or requests for help. They tricked victims into visiting phishing sites that looked like Google login or Google Meet pages, designed to steal email credentials and two-factor authentication (2FA) codes.

The phishing kit used advanced methods like React-based web apps, Web Sockets, and keylogging, and could relay 2FA codes in real time. Some pages were hosted on Google Sites to look more authentic Check Point says this shows APT35’s continued use of social engineering, rapid infrastructure changes, and targeted deception—especially during times of geopolitical conflict.

APT35 Reloaded: Unpacking the Full Chain from Click to Control

Since late 2023, Mint Sandstorm (APT35) has been targeting high-profile academics and researchers across multiple countries using well-crafted phishing emails. The group uses fake journalist personas and compromised email accounts to build trust before delivering malicious RAR files with double-extension payloads. These drop custom backdoors like MediaPl and

MischiefTut, enabling persistence, data collection, and remote command execution. The campaign shows advanced social engineering, stealthy malware delivery, and a strong focus on Middle East policy intelligence.

1. initial Access - Attackers (a subset of Mint Sandstorm) send phishing emails containing malicious links leading to fake or compromised websites.

2. Payload Delivery - Victims who click are tricked into downloading .rar archive files that appear legitimate.

3. Deception via Double Extensions - These archives contain files with double extensions like .pdf.lnk to fool users into thinking they're opening a document, but it's really a shortcut executing code.

4. Execution & Callback - Clicking the file executes a malicious .vbs script, often renamed as a legitimate tool like NirCmd, which connects to Mint Sandstorm- controlled infrastructure.

5. Persistence - Once the malware runs, it establishes persistence by setting scheduled tasks or registry run keys to survive reboots and stay on the system

Charming Kitten Targets Senior Medical Researchers in "BadBlood"

In late 2020, Iranian-linked APT group Charming Kitten launched a targeted phishing campaign aimed at stealing credentials from 25 high- ranking medical researchers in the U.S. and Israel. The operation, dubbed "BadBlood" by Proofpoint researchers, focused on professionals in the fields of genetics, neurology, and oncology.

This campaign marks a notable shift in Charming Kitten’s traditional targeting, which typically focuses on dissidents, diplomats, and journalists aligned with Iranian geopolitical interests. While the group’s exact motives remain unclear, analysts suggest this may have been a short-term intelligence-gathering effort aligned with rising cyber interest in medical research.

BadBlood aligns with a broader trend of threat actors increasingly targeting healthcare and scientific sectors, highlighting the growing importance of securing intellectual property and sensitive research from state-sponsored cyber espionage.

Charming Kitten Target Journalists with Fake News Outlets"

Charming Kitten has been targeting international Persian-language media and journalists with phishing and intimidation tactics, often orchestrated through fake news agencies like “The British news agency.” Their campaigns aim to harass, monitor, and manipulate reporters, highlighting the group’s persistent efforts to control news coverage and silence critical voices abroad.

group creates convincing fake news pages to build credibility and earn the trust of visitors, encouraging them to stay on the site longer. This extended engagement is crucial because it allows the embedded BeEF (Browser Exploitation Framework) tool more time to search for and

exploit vulnerabilities in the victim’s browser. BeEF is a powerful open-source tool commonly used in penetration testing, capable of automating attacks and probing for weaknesses while

the victim unknowingly browses the site. By combining social engineering with technical exploitation, the group significantly increases its chances of successfully infiltrating target

systems.

Charming Kitten often targets individuals researching Iran by creating fake online personas, typically presenting themselves as students or journalists. These fabricated accounts reach out to potential victims through email or social media, aiming to establish trust and initiate contact. In one instance, a fake account named Zehavit Yehuda sent an email containing a link generated via Google Sites, which adds an extra layer of credibility because it appears to be a legitimate, Google-approved address. This strategy combines social engineering with the use of reputable online platforms, making it more likely that recipients will trust and interact with the

malicious content.

Charming Kitten employs a tactic of impersonating trusted figures—such as students or journalists—by crafting fake online identities to approach individuals researching Iran. These deceptive personas initiate contact through email or social media, attempting to build rapport and gain the trust of their targets. For example, a fabricated account under the name Zehavit Yehuda sent an email that included a link created with Google Sites. The use of a Google- approved service lends additional credibility to the message, making recipients more likely to view it as legitimate and engage with the link. This approach skillfully blends social engineering with the exploitation of reputable online platforms, increasing the likelihood that victims will interact with malicious content without suspicion.

The Download button is a redirection link: http://www.google[.]com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fdownload- google.comorginallinks.ga%2Fdownload%2Ffile%2Fusr%<redacted>&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=<redac ted> Which leads to a fake log-in page in a domain registered by the attackers: http://download-google.com-orginal-links[.]ga/download/file/usr/<redacted>

The Charming Kitten group creates fake websites that impersonate real organizations and companies, using these sites to distribute malicious files or launch attacks on target systems with tools like BeEF. Notably, they have been reported to mimic major firms such as “United Technologies,” which operates in the fields of aircraft engines, space systems, and defense. By copying the identities of reputable institutions, the group aims to gain the trust of their victims and increase the effectiveness of their social engineering and technical exploitation tactics.

Charming Kitten uses fake Google Drive file-sharing links, created through Google Sites, to trick users into believing they are accessing legitimate files. This method exploits users’ trust in Google services, making phishing attempts more convincing and helping attackers steal information or deliver malware.

inside Charming Kitten’s Phishing Methods: Gmail and Yahoo Impersonation Attacks

the group created an email address named suspended.user.notification[at]gmail.com and appears to have conducted their attacks through this account. The tactic they used here involves telling the target that their account has been suspended and that they need to click a link and log in. When the target clicks the link, they are redirected to the following login page, where the attackers attempt to steal their credentials.

It has been reported that the Charming Kitten group uses a wide variety of techniques. Below are some examples of the techniques they use, along with screenshots:

  • A phishing email sent by impersonating the Google Hangouts service
  • An email claiming there has been suspicious activity on your account and asking whether you performed this activity
  • A fake site imitating Google’s 2-Step Verification service, aiming to steal the SMS sent to the user
  • The group is also seen impersonating Yahoo services, with a fake login page that appears to belong to Yahoo Mail
  • The group has also imitated Yahoo’s 2-Step Verification service

Phishing emails were distributed to hundreds of targets from the unfamiliar address mails.customerservices@gmail.com, featuring a malicious link to goo- gle[.]mobi. The messages, shown in the attached screenshots, are not direct copies of official Google notifications. Instead, they display spelling and grammatical mistakes, with certain errors—like the use of direct speech in place of indirect speech—reflecting patterns common among Persian speakers.

8. Phishing Infrastructure

A phishing campaign operating from September to November 2018 utilized an extensive network of over 20 malicious domains, with the infrastructure continuing to expand during the research period. The scale and rapid deployment of these interconnected domains demonstrated the attackers' sophisticated approach and significant resource investment in this operation
